catalog_quote: Unlike the prosodic systems of the Yupik languages, CG is not a system of stress assignment. Word stress is assigned after CG applies, with no consideration of whether a given syllable has or has not been altered by CG. Whereas CG affects alternate syllables, as explained below, resembling Yupik prosody in this respect, word stress is assigned individually to syllables practically regardless of what precedes or follows. The basic stress rule for King Island Inupiaq is that the non-final closed syllables and all long vowels—including diphthongs and vowel clusters, which are phonetically long—receive stress. Thus, áiviq 'walrus', íglu 'sod or rock house', and Inúktuyúuq, a personal name. Whereas long vowels (aa, ii, and uu) and diphthongs (ai [e:] and au [o:]) are stressed uniformly throughout their entire quantity, vowel clusters (iu, ui, ia, ua) receive stress on their second member, e.g. puítuq 'it is swollen', except in a word-final syllable, e.g. úi 'husband' and niγiřúaq 'one who is eating'. A long consonant, like a consonant cluster, has the effect of closing the preceding syllable, e.g. mánnik 'egg'. Long consonants may be underlying, as in mannik, or may result from CG. In iřítuq [iřít:uq] 'it fell', whose syllables would otherwise be equally stressless, CG has the effect of lengthening the t and closing the preceding syllable, which is then stressed.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Non-culminative, quantity-driven stress: every heavy syllable is stressed -- any non-final syllable closed by a consonant cluster or long (geminate) consonant, and any syllable with a long vowel, diphthong or vowel cluster (final or not). Light open syllables are unstressed; a word consisting only of light syllables plus a final closed syllable has no stressed syllable ('equally stressless') unless Consonant Gradation lengthens a consonant and thereby closes a syllable. Stress is assigned after, and independently of, the alternating strong/weak 'syllable strength' pattern that drives Consonant Gradation; no single primary-stress position is designated.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None distinguished; all heavy syllables are described as receiving stress equally, with no primary/secondary ranking. (Kaplan separately notes single consonants become fortis/long after a 'strong' syllable, but stresses this strength is not phonetic stress.)
new_statements.exceptions: Word-final closed syllables are not stressed by closure alone (only 'non-final closed syllables'); vowel clusters take stress on their second member except in a word-final syllable, where the first member is stressed (úi, niγiřúaq); Consonant Gradation can feed or bleed stress by closing or opening syllables (iřítuq [iřít:uq]; KI igáyatuq from /ikayuqtuq/). Rule stated for King Island; CG output differs in Diomede, Wales, Qawiaraq but no different stress rule is given for them.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on isolated word forms (citation forms with acute accents); explicitly distinguished from the abstract 'syllable strength' governing Consonant Gradation and from Yupik rhythmic stress. No phrase-level discussion.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted rule is stated explicitly for King Island Inupiaq (Ugiuvak), one sub-dialect of the Bering Strait dialect of Seward Peninsula Inupiaq (nort2945; Glottolog dialect node for King Island is under Bering Strait Inupiatun). Kaplan presents King Island as representative of the Seward Peninsula group and says stress is assigned syllable-by-syllable independently of Consonant Gradation; he does not restate the stress rule separately for Diomede, Wales or Qawiaraq. NB: Glottolog's only 'grammar' for nort2945, Lanz 2010, actually describes the Malimiut Coastal dialect, which is North Alaskan Inupiaq (nort2944), not Seward Peninsula; it also gives no placement rule.

new_statements.quote: [S]tress as such is not a predominant feature of the language, but its underlying existence can clearly be seen in the consonant weakening rules [...] Seward Peninsula Inupiaq and Alaskan Yupik are characterized by the same basic stress rules as Siberian Yupik, with one important addition: initial closed short syllables are stressed (isogloss 5). Thus the stress rules of both may be stated as follows: 1. Primary stress: long syllables and initial closed short syllables are stressed. 2. Rhythmic stress: every other syllable of a series of short syllables following a primarily stressed syllable or the beginning of the word is stressed. 3. Final syllables are destressed.

new_statements.relation_note: Same type as the catalog (weight-sensitive: long syllables and closed syllables attract prominence) and adds the rhythmic alternation, the no-final-stress and no-secondary-stress details. But Leer's 'stress rules' are explicitly an abstract syllable-weight system underlying consonant weakening ('stress as such is not a predominant feature'), whereas the catalog's Kaplan 1985 statement is about surface word stress and says the alternating strong/weak pattern is NOT stress ('CG is not a system of stress assignment.. word stress is assigned individually to syllables practically regardless of what precedes or follows'; non-final closed syllables and all long vowels are stressed). Concretely the…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Leer treats the syllable-weight system that drives Seward Peninsula consonant weakening as an (underlying) stress system identical to the basic Alaskan Yupik rules: long syllables and word-initial closed short syllables carry primary stress; among runs of short syllables every other one is stressed (rhythmic alternation, restated in draft 2 as: if a word begins with two short syllables and the first is not stressed, the second is; after a stressed syllable the second of two short syllables is stressed, recursively); final syllables are never stressed. Draft 2 p.28 restates rule 1 as 'Non-rhythmic stress: long syllables and initial short closed syllables are stressed.' The flow chart (f.1 p.60 = f.2 p.91) makes the same procedure explicit: stress the initial syllable if closed or long, otherwise the second; then iterate, stressing a long S1, else S2, stopping at the word boundary.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None in SPI: draft f.2 p.31 says 'There are three related prosodic phenomena found in all Alaskan Yupik which do not occur in Seward Peninsula Inupiaq' - rhythmic lengthening, secondary stress and e-compensation are 'peculiar to Alaskan Yupik'.
new_statements.exceptions: No stress-skipping rule in SPI (f.1 p.15 / f.2 p.29: 'In Kotlik Central Yupik and Seward Peninsula Inupiaq, however, there are no stress-skipping rules'); unlike St. Lawrence Island Yupik the initial short closed syllable is stressed (f.2 p.29). Final syllables destressed. Leer's dialect table covers King Island, Teller Spit, Wales-Shishmaref, Little Diomede; draft 2 p.8 says the SPI weight rules hold for 'King Island, Teller Spit, Wales, Shishmaref, and the Diomede Islands'.
new_statements.identity_note: The catalog's Kaplan 1985 statement is specifically about King Island (Ugiuvak) Inupiaq, 'representative of CG in its fullest form'. Leer 1977 covers Seward Peninsula Inupiaq as a group (King Island, Teller Spit, Wales-Shishmaref, Little Diomede in his dialect table; draft 2 p.8 adds 'the Diomede Islands'). Leer 1974-75 p.5 describes one Fish River (White Mountain) speaker, i.e. the eastern Qawiaraq-area dialect, where Kaplan 1985 says consonant gradation is nearly non-productive; Leer's other 1974 sections (Koyuk, Mary's Igloo, Teller, Shishmaref) say nothing about stress.

new_statements.quote: Also, I seemed to notice that he had a Yupik-like way of stressing alternate open short syllables, but rather than lengthen the vowels in the stressed syllables, he would make the following consonant somewhat fortis. I might have written these double had I not known the structure of the word. I feel that perhaps we are dealing with a fortis versus lenis distinction, if any, rather than geminated consonants, in some cases in this dialect. Other than this, there was no consonant weakening either in Percy's dialect or in the neighboring Mary's Igloo dialect.

readall_conflicts: Leer ca. 1977 and the catalog's Kaplan 1985 statement disagree on what counts as stress, not on the data. Leer calls the Yupik-style alternating syllable-weight pattern (long syllables and initial closed short syllables strong; every other short syllable thereafter strong; final syllable never strong) the stress rules of Seward Peninsula Inupiaq, while conceding that 'stress as such is not a predominant feature of the language'. Kaplan 1985 (p. 193) describes the same alternating strong/weak pattern as 'syllable strength' governing consonant gradation and says explicitly that it 'is not a system of stress assignment'; surface word stress is assigned locally to every non-final closed syllable and every long vowel. Taken as placement rules the two differ (e.g. a word CV.CV.CVC.CV gets Leer's rhythmic stress on syllable 2 but Kaplan's surface stress on syllable 3; Leer stresses only initial closed short syllables non-rhythmically, Kaplan all non-final closed syllables). Both are weight-sensitive; the catalog should keep Kaplan 1985 as the surface-stress statement and note Leer 1977 as the underlying-weight analysis. Leer 1974-75 (Fish River speaker, alternating stress on short open syllables) is a tentative note on a different sub-dialect and does not conflict with either. Kaplan 1990 and Kaplan 1988 could not be opened (not reachable by automated download and lending-only respectively), so their statements are unknown.
